newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore poll guessing game a double-edged sword.
newsitem.headline: Singapore poll guessing game a double-edged sword.

text.p: The guessing game over dates for Singapore's general election could be a double-edged sword for the ruling People's Action Party (PAP), analysts and opposition members said on Tuesday.

A date remains elusive, despite an announcement on Monday that parliament had been dissolved. The government followed that by setting December 23 as the last day for nominations of candidates for the 83-seat parliament.
The announcements sent analysts heading to their calendar. General elections, which must be held by April, have to be held within three months of the dissolution of parliament.
They can be held a minimum of nine days -- or a maximum of eight weeks -- after the nomination date.

As the PAP, which has won every election in Singapore since 1959, has usually favoured the nine day minimum to give the opposition as little time to campaign as possible, most analysts see an election date soon after January 2, the ninth day.
However the announcements of nomination day and an election date have usually been made together.

And Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, who has teased reporters for months over election dates, was still not telling. He has said he would decide on dates after "smelling the air" in an opposition constituency this weekend.
"We had expected elections to be called earlier and have been preparing for the past two years," said Tan Chee Kien, President of the opposition National Solidarity Party.
"The delay in announcing the date is actually giving us more time to look for more credible people to stand for elections."
But political scientist Hussin Mutalib said that not announcing polling date along with the nomination date could be a deliberate attempt by Goh to force the opposition to reveal their candidates.
He could be planning an election date several weeks away, giving the PAP time to scrutinise the opposition candidates and figure out their weaknesses, Hussin said.
PAP candidate Hawazi Daipi, who reckoned on early January elections, did not see it that way.
"I don't see any remarkable strategy to put the opposition off balance," he said. "If they had been ready for the hustings, they should not be worried about the recent government move."

Constitutional lawyer Kevin Tan said the delay might not give the opposition enough time to attract more candidates, needed because of recent changes to the multi-member group representation constituency (GRC).

In these, the winning party gets all the seats. They have a maximum of six seats, meaning the opposition has to put up that many people. The opposition has always had difficulty finding enough candidates.
Hawazi said the more time the opposition was given, the more effectively they would be able to campaign.
Tan Chee Kien said the delay in announcing the election date revealed the PAP's lack of confidence, and Hussin said there might be some truth to that.
"The Singapore electorate is in some ways predictable, meaning they want the PAP government to continue," he said.

"But they are also a volatile, highly mobile electorate in the sense of the unpredictability of where they want to give their votes. I think there is a certain amount of jitters on the part of the PAP of not knowing where their support is," he said.
Hussin said there might be similarities between the coming elections and that of 1984, when the PAP paraded a large team of new candidates it described as its best so far.
"Yet the PAP suffered a humiliating 13-percent swing in 1984. With all these new candidates, there is no guarantee it will mean a better performance for the PAP" in 1997, he said.
